# Partitions and QOS on MedicineBow {#sec-partitions}

::: {.tldr}
Two knobs decide where and how your job runs. A **partition** picks the *hardware* (plain
CPU nodes, H100 GPUs, the big absorbed Teton pool, …). A **QOS** picks the *service tier* —
how long you may run, how much you may grab, and how high your priority is. The trade-off is
clean: **the longer the walltime you ask for, the lower your priority and the smaller your
allowed footprint.** Choosing well is the subject of @sec-queue-times.
:::

## Partition = which hardware

A partition is a named pool of nodes. Submit with `--partition=<name>` (the default is `mb`).
Here's what's actually on the machine:

| Partition | Nodes | Cores/node | Mem/node | GPUs/node | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **`mb`** *(default)* | 25 | 96 (EPYC 9454) | ~1023 GB | — | general CPU work |
| `mb-h100` | 6 | 96 | ~1281 GB | 8× **H100** | large model training, PINNs |
| `mb-l40s` | 4 | 96 | ~765 GB | 8× L40S¹ | inference, mid-size training |
| `mb-a30` | 8 | 96 | ~765 GB | 8× A30 | dev/GPU, smaller models |
| `mb-a6000` | 1 | 64 | ~1023 GB | 4× A6000 | GPU dev |
| `mb-r6000` | 3 | 72 | ~515 GB | 4× R6000 | GPU dev |
| `debug` | 4 | 28 | ~128 GB | — | quick tests (pair with `debug` QOS) |
| `teton` | ~250 | 32 | ~120 GB+ | — | large CPU throughput, arrays |
| `beartooth` | 9 | 56 | ~257 GB+ | — | CPU work |
| `wildiris` | 5 | 48 | ~507 GB+ | — | CPU work |
| `non-investor` | 110 | mixed | mixed | — | **CPU work you don't want preempted** |
| `non-investor-gpu` | 7 | mixed | mixed | mixed | **GPU work you don't want preempted** |
| `inv-*` | varies | varies | varies | varies | investor-owned; borrowable but **preemptible** |

<small>¹ One L40S node has 4 GPUs instead of 8. Numbers are the machine as observed in July 2026; verify current state with `showpartitions` and `sinfo`.</small>

*Teton, Beartooth, and WildIris* are the old retired clusters, now living on as big
partitions inside MedicineBow — Teton alone is ~250 nodes, which is why it swallows so much
throughput work. The `inv-*` partitions are **investor ("condo") hardware**: you can run on
them when they're idle, but the owner can reclaim the node and bump your job (@sec-preemption).

::: {.callout-note}
## Avoiding preemption: use `non-investor`, not `--constraint`
Some docs tell you to add `--constraint=non-investor` to avoid running on preemptible
investor hardware. **That constraint matches nothing on the current machine and silently does
nothing.** The real mechanism is a **partition**: submit to `--partition=non-investor` (110
CPU nodes) or `--partition=non-investor-gpu` (7 GPU nodes) to stay on hardware that won't be
reclaimed out from under you. This is the correct home for long, un-checkpointed runs.
:::

You can list several partitions and let Slurm use whichever frees up first —
`--partition=mb,teton,beartooth` is common for CPU throughput work and is exactly what the
busiest jobs on the machine do.

## QOS = which service tier

A **Quality of Service** sets three things at once: your **maximum walltime**, your **CPU
footprint cap**, and your **priority**. Submit with `--qos=<name>` (the default is `normal`).

| QOS | Priority | Max walltime | CPU cap / account | Your project can use it? |
|---|---:|---|---:|:---:|
| `interactive` | 90 | 8 h | 4746 | ✅ |
| `fast` | 80 | 12 h | 4746 | ✅ |
| `normal` *(default)* | 70 | 3 d | 4746 | ✅ |
| `long` | 60 | 7 d | 2876 | ✅ |
| `debug` | 0 | 1 h | 7 cpu / 32 G / 2 nodes | ✅ |
| `extended` | 50 | 14 d | 2157 | ❌ (not granted) |
| `inv-*` (investor) | 110 | 14 d | varies | ❌ (owners only) |

Confirm your own list any time:

```bash
sacctmgr -n show assoc user=$USER format=qos
# cowy-firesurro:  debug, fast, interactive, long, normal
sqos                         # full QOS table with limits
```

::: {.callout-important}
## The core trade-off, in one sentence
**The longer the walltime you ask for, the lower your priority *and* the smaller your allowed
footprint.** `fast` (12 h) gives you priority 80 and the full 4746-core cap. `long` (7 d)
drops you to priority 60 and a ~40%-smaller cap. You pay for patience with priority, and for
size with time. This single fact drives every recommendation in @sec-queue-times.
:::

## `DenyOnLimit`: rejected at submit, not stuck forever

Every QOS is flagged **`DenyOnLimit`**. If you ask for more than a QOS allows — say a 5-day
run under `normal` (max 3 d), or more cores than the cap — Slurm **rejects the job the moment
you submit it**, with a clear error. It does *not* silently queue it forever. That's good
news: you find out immediately, fix the request, and resubmit.

## Putting both knobs in a script

```bash
#SBATCH --partition=mb          # hardware: general CPU nodes
#SBATCH --qos=fast              # tier: 12h max, high priority
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00         # within the fast 12h ceiling
```

For a GPU job:

```bash
#SBATCH --partition=mb-l40s
#SBATCH --qos=normal
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1            # ask for 1 GPU (see @sec-gpu)
#SBATCH --time=08:00:00
```

Now — *which* combination should you actually pick? That depends entirely on whether you're
doing a quick proof-of-concept or a long production run, and how busy each queue is right
now. That's the next chapter, and it's the one to read carefully.
